---
title: "Bayesian linear regression"
execute:
  enabled: true
  echo: true
  warning: false
  message: false
---

The Provo Gaussian linear model can be combined with a prior to produce a posterior distribution over regression lines. Recall from [posterior distributions](../statistical-inference/posterior-distributions.qmd) that updating multiplies a likelihood by a prior and then normalizes the product. The response model remains the Gaussian specification stated below.

The [Provo measurement discussion](regression-models.qmd#provo-word-position-data) defines each response as a word position mean of log first fixation durations among readers with a retained positive fixation. It defines modeled cloze surprisal as the negative base-two logarithm of a fitted cloze probability. Skipped reader--word trials do not enter that mean, and the available table retains passage grouping rather than reader identities.

The likelihood is the joint density of the fixed observed responses viewed as a function of unknown parameters, as defined on the [maximum likelihood page](../statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd). Its factorization uses [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd); its covariance matrix records [variances and covariances](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd). The [Monte Carlo page](../statistical-inference/monte-carlo-integration.qmd) later explains how averages over posterior draws approximate integrals. A [residual](residuals.qmd) remains observed minus fitted response, now evaluated across posterior draws when uncertainty is propagated.

The derivation has three parts: we first specify a conjugate prior, then update its parameters from the likelihood, and finally compute posterior summaries and fitted means.

$$
\mathbf Y\mid\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2
\sim
\mathcal N(\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2\mathbf I).
$$

What changes is that uncertainty about $\boldsymbol\beta$ and $\sigma^2$ is represented before and after observing the responses.

## A conjugate prior specification

We use the normal--inverse-gamma specification

$$
\boldsymbol\beta\mid\sigma^2
\sim
\mathcal N(\mathbf b_0,\sigma^2\mathbf V_0)
$$

and

$$
\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{InverseGamma}(a_0,d_0).
$$

We use the shape--scale parameterization

$$
p(\sigma^2)
\propto
(\sigma^2)^{-(a_0+1)}
\exp\left(-\frac{d_0}{\sigma^2}\right),
$$

whose mean is $d_0/(a_0-1)$ when $a_0>1$. Conditional conjugacy is useful here because it makes every updating step visible. It is not a claim that a normal--inverse-gamma prior is required for regression.

## From likelihood and prior to posterior

The basic algebra is **completing the square**: rewriting a quadratic so that
its center is visible. Begin with one coefficient and suppress the common scale
factor. Combining one squared data discrepancy with a normal prior discrepancy
gives

$$
(y-\beta)^2+\frac{(\beta-b_0)^2}{v_0}
=
\left(1+\frac{1}{v_0}\right)\beta^2
-2\left(y+\frac{b_0}{v_0}\right)\beta
+\text{terms without }\beta.
$$

Write \(A=1+1/v_0\) and \(h=y+b_0/v_0\). Then

$$
A\beta^2-2h\beta
=
A\left(\beta-\frac{h}{A}\right)^2
-\frac{h^2}{A}.
$$

The coefficient \(A\) is the **precision**, the inverse of the variance, and
\(h\) is an **information value** that combines the prior center with the data.
Their ratio \(h/A\) is the updated center. The matrix derivation below performs
this same operation for several coefficients at once: precision becomes a
matrix and the information value becomes a vector.

The likelihood kernel is

$$
p(\mathbf y\mid\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2)
\propto
(\sigma^2)^{-n/2}
\exp\left[
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)^\top
(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)
\right].
$$

Multiplying by the conditional normal prior adds the quadratic

$$
(\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf b_0)^\top
\mathbf V_0^{-1}
(\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf b_0).
$$

Collect the terms involving $\boldsymbol\beta$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\boldsymbol\beta^\top
(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X+\mathbf V_0^{-1})
\boldsymbol\beta\\
&\quad-2\boldsymbol\beta^\top
(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf y+\mathbf V_0^{-1}\mathbf b_0)
+\mathbf y^\top\mathbf y
+\mathbf b_0^\top\mathbf V_0^{-1}\mathbf b_0.
\end{aligned}
$$

Define

$$
\mathbf V_n^{-1}=\mathbf V_0^{-1}+\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X,
\qquad
\mathbf V_n^{-1}\mathbf b_n
=\mathbf V_0^{-1}\mathbf b_0+\mathbf X^\top\mathbf y.
$$

Thus \(\mathbf V_n^{-1}\) is the posterior **precision matrix**, and
\(\mathbf V_0^{-1}\mathbf b_0+\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf y\) is the
posterior **information vector**. Multiplying that vector by the covariance
\(\mathbf V_n\) recovers the posterior center \(\mathbf b_n\), just as \(h/A\)
did in the scalar calculation.

Completing the square yields

$$
(\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf b_n)^\top
\mathbf V_n^{-1}
(\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf b_n)
+
\mathbf y^\top\mathbf y
+\mathbf b_0^\top\mathbf V_0^{-1}\mathbf b_0
-\mathbf b_n^\top\mathbf V_n^{-1}\mathbf b_n.
$$

The first term is the kernel of the updated conditional normal distribution. The remaining scalar joins the inverse-gamma scale. Thus the posterior parameters are the quantities left by completing the square.

The posterior is again normal--inverse-gamma, with

$$
\mathbf V_n
=
(\mathbf V_0^{-1}+\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)^{-1},
$$

$$
\mathbf b_n
=
\mathbf V_n
(\mathbf V_0^{-1}\mathbf b_0+\mathbf X^\top\mathbf y),
$$

$$
a_n=a_0+\frac n2,
$$

and

$$
d_n
=
d_0+\frac12
\left(
\mathbf y^\top\mathbf y
+\mathbf b_0^\top\mathbf V_0^{-1}\mathbf b_0
-\mathbf b_n^\top\mathbf V_n^{-1}\mathbf b_n
\right).
$$

## Computing the posterior

Before drawing all coefficients, consider two independent standard-normal
coordinates \(z_1\) and \(z_2\). Define two coefficient deviations by

$$
\delta_1=z_1,
\qquad
\delta_2=0.8z_1+0.6z_2. % dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
$$

The second deviation shares \(z_1\) with the first. Both deviations have
variance one, while their covariance is \(0.8\). The same calculation can be
written

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\delta_1\\\delta_2\end{bmatrix}
=
\underbrace{
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0\\ % dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
0.8&0.6 % dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
\end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf L}
\begin{bmatrix}z_1\\z_2\end{bmatrix}. % dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
$$

The lower-triangular matrix \(\mathbf L\) is a mixing recipe: it turns
independent coordinates into deviations having covariance

$$
\mathbf L\mathbf L^{\mathsf T}
=
\begin{bmatrix}1&0.8\\0.8&1\end{bmatrix}. % dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
$$

The [matrix
primer](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd#vectors-matrices-and-covariance)
shows how the two row-by-column calculations in this product arise from scalar
multiplication and addition. The figure applies the same mixing recipe to every
point on a circular contour.

~~~{r}
#| label: fig-cholesky-circle-to-ellipse
#| fig-cap: "A lower-triangular mixing matrix transforms an independent-coordinate circle into a tilted correlated ellipse."
#| fig-alt: "Two coordinate panels. The first contains a circular contour for two independent standard-normal coordinates. The second contains a narrow ellipse tilted upward, showing positive covariance between the transformed coefficient deviations."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.4

library(ggplot2)

angle <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 241L) # dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
independent_contour <- cbind(cos(angle), sin(angle))
L_example <- matrix(
  c(1, 0, 0.8, 0.6), # dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
  nrow = 2,
  byrow = TRUE
)
correlated_contour <- t(L_example %*% t(independent_contour))

cholesky_plot <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    coordinate_1 = independent_contour[, 1],
    coordinate_2 = independent_contour[, 2],
    stage = "Independent coordinates"
  ),
  data.frame(
    coordinate_1 = correlated_contour[, 1],
    coordinate_2 = correlated_contour[, 2],
    stage = "Correlated deviations"
  )
)

ggplot(cholesky_plot, aes(coordinate_1, coordinate_2)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey85", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey85", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_path(color = "#2C6E9B", linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~stage) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-1.15, 1.15), ylim = c(-1.15, 1.15)) +
  labs(x = "Coordinate 1", y = "Coordinate 2") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 11)
~~~

We call a lower-triangular mixing matrix with this property a **Cholesky
factor**. In general, \(\mathbf L\) satisfies
\(\mathbf V_n=\mathbf L\mathbf L^{\mathsf T}\). R's `chol(Vn)` returns the
upper-triangular transpose \(\mathbf R=\mathbf L^{\mathsf T}\). Because the code
stores independent draws as rows, multiplying them on the right by
\(\mathbf R\) gives covariance
\(\mathbf R^{\mathsf T}\mathbf R=\mathbf V_n\).

```{r}
#| label: fit-provo-bayesian-regression
library(ggplot2)

provo <- read.csv(
  "data/provo/content-word-positions.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
provo$cloze_surprisal_bits <- -log2(provo$OrthoMatchModel)
provo$cloze_surprisal_c <-
  provo$cloze_surprisal_bits - mean(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits)

ols_fit <- lm(mean_log_ffd ~ cloze_surprisal_c, data = provo)
X <- model.matrix(ols_fit)
y <- provo$mean_log_ffd
residual_scale <- summary(ols_fit)$sigma

b0 <- c(mean(y), 0)
V0 <- diag(c(
  (2 * sd(y) / residual_scale)^2,
  (2 * sd(y) / (sd(provo$cloze_surprisal_c) * residual_scale))^2
))
a0 <- ncol(X) + 1
d0 <- (a0 - 1) * residual_scale^2

Vn <- solve(solve(V0) + crossprod(X))
bn <- drop(Vn %*% (solve(V0) %*% b0 + crossprod(X, y)))
an <- a0 + nrow(provo) / 2
dn <- as.numeric(
  d0 + .5 * (
    crossprod(y) +
      t(b0) %*% solve(V0) %*% b0 -
      t(bn) %*% solve(Vn) %*% bn
  )
)

set.seed(20261019)
n_draws <- 4000L
sigma2_draws <- 1 / rgamma(n_draws, shape = an, rate = dn)
beta_noise <- matrix(
  rnorm(n_draws * ncol(X)),
  nrow = n_draws
) %*% chol(Vn)
beta_draws <- matrix(
  bn,
  nrow = n_draws,
  ncol = ncol(X),
  byrow = TRUE
) + sweep(beta_noise, 1, sqrt(sigma2_draws), `*`)
colnames(beta_draws) <- colnames(X)

slope_interval <- quantile(
  beta_draws[, "cloze_surprisal_c"],
  c(.025, .975)
)

stopifnot(
  all(is.finite(beta_draws)),
  all(is.finite(sigma2_draws)),
  slope_interval[[1]] < slope_interval[[2]]
)

data.frame(
  posterior_mean_slope = mean(beta_draws[, "cloze_surprisal_c"]),
  posterior_sd_slope = sd(beta_draws[, "cloze_surprisal_c"]),
  lower = slope_interval[[1]],
  upper = slope_interval[[2]]
)
```

The code mirrors the algebra: `Vn` inverts prior precision plus data precision;
`bn` multiplies that covariance by the prior-and-data information vector; `an`
adds $n/2$; and `dn` is the constant left after completing the square. Because
$1/\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(a_n,d_n)$ under this parameterization,
`1 / rgamma(..., rate = dn)` generates inverse-gamma draws.

Scaling the transformed standard-normal vector by the sampled \(\sigma\) and
adding \(\mathbf b_n\) produces one draw from the conditional multivariate
normal posterior.

The 4,000 draws determine the Monte Carlo precision of our summaries. They do
not enter the inferential assumptions. For a posterior mean, simulation error is
approximately the posterior draw SD divided by $\sqrt{4000}$ because these
conjugate draws are independent. More draws reduce numerical error but do not
change the posterior distribution.

The posterior mean slope is `r sprintf("%.6f", mean(beta_draws[, "cloze_surprisal_c"]))`, with a central interval from `r sprintf("%.6f", slope_interval[[1]])` to `r sprintf("%.6f", slope_interval[[2]])`.

The coefficient-prior location and scale use the observed Provo response and predictor scales. The inverse-gamma shape is one plus the observed design dimension, and its scale sets the prior mean of $\sigma^2$ to the OLS residual variance. These data-dependent priors are useful for connecting conjugate algebra to regression, but they are not independently specified confirmatory priors.

The following prior predictive calculation makes that limitation visible. It draws parameters from the data-calibrated prior and a response at centered surprisal before conditioning on the likelihood.

```{r}
#| label: check-provo-prior-predictive
set.seed(20261018)
n_prior_draws <- 1000L
prior_sigma2 <- 1 / rgamma(n_prior_draws, shape = a0, rate = d0) # dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
prior_beta_noise <- matrix(
  rnorm(n_prior_draws * ncol(X)),
  nrow = n_prior_draws
) %*% chol(V0)
prior_beta <- matrix(
  b0,
  nrow = n_prior_draws,
  ncol = ncol(X),
  byrow = TRUE
) + sweep(prior_beta_noise, 1L, sqrt(prior_sigma2), `*`)
colnames(prior_beta) <- colnames(X)
prior_mean_at_center <- prior_beta[, "(Intercept)"]
prior_response_at_center <- prior_mean_at_center +
  rnorm(n_prior_draws, sd = sqrt(prior_sigma2))

data.frame(
  quantity = c("mean at centered surprisal", "new response at centered surprisal"),
  lower = c(
    quantile(prior_mean_at_center, .025),
    quantile(prior_response_at_center, .025)
  ),
  median = c(
    median(prior_mean_at_center),
    median(prior_response_at_center)
  ),
  upper = c(
    quantile(prior_mean_at_center, .975),
    quantile(prior_response_at_center, .975)
  )
)
```

A [prior predictive check](../statistical-inference/prior-predictive-distributions.qmd) ordinarily precedes looking at the responses. Here it documents the implications of a prior already calibrated to those responses; it cannot retroactively make the prior independent of the sample.

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-bayesian-regression
#| fig-cap: "Provo positions with the posterior mean line and a central posterior interval for the conditional mean."
grid <- data.frame(
  cloze_surprisal_bits = seq(
    min(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits),
    max(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits),
    length.out = 160L
  )
)
grid$cloze_surprisal_c <-
  grid$cloze_surprisal_bits - mean(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits)
mu_draws <- outer(
  beta_draws[, "cloze_surprisal_c"],
  grid$cloze_surprisal_c,
  `*`
)
mu_draws <- sweep(mu_draws, 1, beta_draws[, "(Intercept)"], `+`)
grid$posterior_mean <- colMeans(mu_draws)
grid$lower <- apply(mu_draws, 2, quantile, probs = .025)
grid$upper <- apply(mu_draws, 2, quantile, probs = .975)

point_opacity <- 0.2
interval_opacity <- 0.2
ggplot(provo, aes(cloze_surprisal_bits, mean_log_ffd)) +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = grid,
    aes(x = cloze_surprisal_bits, ymin = lower, ymax = upper),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    fill = "#2C6E9B",
    alpha = interval_opacity
  ) +
  geom_point(color = "grey65", alpha = point_opacity, size = 0.8) +
  geom_line(
    data = grid,
    aes(y = posterior_mean),
    color = "#2C6E9B",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Modeled cloze surprisal (bits)",
    y = "Mean log first fixation duration"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The posterior represents uncertainty under the same aggregated position likelihood. Bayesian updating does not restore participant observations or make the association causal.

## Recap and check your understanding

1. Which part of the model is shared with OLS?
2. Why is this not a confirmatory prior analysis?
3. Why are predictions computed for every posterior draw?
4. Which data limitation survives the Bayesian formulation?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The Gaussian linear response model, including the straight conditional mean and common independent residual variance, is shared with OLS. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The coefficient and variance priors are calibrated from the observed predictor, response, and OLS residual scales rather than specified independently before seeing the data. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Evaluating the fitted mean within every joint draw propagates posterior covariance among coefficients into uncertainty about the prediction. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The data still contain reader-aggregated position summaries, so participant-level responses and dependence remain unavailable. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
